pass_a_gloss: Of prayers, holy childbearing, and all that Christians must share in common he says marriage is not foreign to God. So I charge—the Lord, not I—that a wife must not leave her husband. The main point: a bond already tied must stay tied. Yet if she leaves—many causes can arise; if she has fornicated, keeping her is itself sin. If she leaves and a cause exists, she must stay single or return to him. Likewise I want husbands not to dismiss wives. To everyone else I speak, I not the Lord. For those already married I do not lay down law—the Lord does; for those not married but yoked to unbelievers I have no divine statute to hand down, for they are not even fit for God’s statutes; yet let them hear us. To clarify the passage I will use what Moses wrote. Some Mosaic statutes are God’s; some are Moses’. Knowing that split, the Lord said of God’s statutes “God said Honor father and mother,” and of Moses’ “Moses allowed you to dismiss wives because of hard hearts.” Keep the divorce booklet and you will see that statute was not written from a Lord’s command. Moses, serving God, gave secondary statutes beside God’s; Paul, serving the gospel, gave secondary statutes to church people after the statutes from God through Jesus Christ. Better to hear the Lord’s statutes than Paul’s. Even if Paul is holy, his statutes stand far below the Lord’s. The unbelieving husband is consecrated in the wife, and the unbelieving wife in the brother. Husband and wife blend into one flesh as wine with water; and as a believer shares holiness with a Gentile spouse—or a believing woman with an unbelieving man—so an unbeliever shares stain with a believing spouse. Why then say the unbeliever is consecrated by receiving from the believer, and not also defiled by receiving from the unbelieving side? Each speaks from the heart’s overflow and either gives or takes, and over time one side wholly wins. What need then of such a fight and risk? He will either succeed or fail, and either lose his soul too or after hard labor barely win. So before anyone is caught, look carefully not only at the present but at what is coming, and either refuse marriage or marry in the Lord. A wife stays bound while her husband lives; if he dies she may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. We skip “only in the Lord” and read only the freedom to marry whom she wishes, no longer pairing the limit. Yet even there, after “only in the Lord,” he checks himself: she is more blessed if she remains so, by my judgment. So Paul, having said the brighter word—“she is consecrated”—left the darker side for us to grasp. Was someone called already circumcised? He must not draw a foreskin. Was someone called uncircumcised? He must not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and foreskin is nothing; what matters is keeping God’s commands. Each must stay in the calling where he was called. It may look as if he dragged circumcision talk beside marriage and chastity out of season, since nobody had asked whether circumcised believers must draw the foreskin or uncircumcised ones must be cut, or about “were you called a slave? Do not worry,” and the rest. Perhaps slavery and freedom stand as a figure for married and unmarried, with “circumcised” naming the man who put away his wife and “uncircumcised” the man who stays married? For as the two become one flesh and wife with husband are one flesh, and the circumcised has put away fleshly things, so the man who put away his wife has as it were cut away his own flesh; so too he names a slave, since elsewhere he says the brother or sister is not enslaved in such cases, as if the married were slaves, through
pass_b_english: of prayers and of holy childbearing and of all things in which Christians must share, he says that marriage is not alien to God. I charge, then—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband. The primary point is this: a yoking that has already been bound must not be loosed. But if she is also separated—for many causes of separation can arise; for example if fornication happens to the wife, it is a sin to keep the wife who has fornicated. If then she is also separated and some cause of separation arises, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband. Likewise I also want a husband to be such that he not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord. To those who have married I do not legislate, but the Lord; to those not married but unequally yoked with unbelievers I do not have a law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of God’s laws; but let them hear us. And I will use what is written in the law to make the matters of the place understood. The laws according to Moses—some are God’s, and some are Moses’. And knowing this difference of God’s laws and Moses’ laws, the Lord said concerning those legislated by God: For God said, Honor father and mother; and concerning those by Moses: Moses, because of your hardness of heart, allowed you to dismiss your wives (Matthew 19:8). If you keep the matters of the book of divorce you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses then, serving God, gave second laws beside the laws of God; Paul, serving the gospel, gave second laws to those of the church after the laws from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, still he has laws far lesser than the laws of the Lord.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy in the brother (1 Corinthians 7:14). As a kind of blending happens of the two, husband and wife, into one flesh, as of wine and water; and as the believer imparts holiness to the Gentile spouse, or the reverse—the believing woman to the unbelieving husband—so also the unbeliever imparts pollution to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. Why then does he say the unbeliever is made holy by receiving something from the believer, and is not also profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving part? For each, conversing from the abundance of the heart with the other, either imparts or receives, and in time the one entirely conquers the other. And what need, he says, of such a contest and danger? For either he will succeed or fail, and either he will lose his soul as well or, after much toil, scarcely be able to gain. Therefore it is good, before a person is forestalled, carefully to look not only at this but also at what is coming, and having looked either not to marry or, marrying, to marry in the Lord. For a wife is bound as long as her husband lives; but if the husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). We do not hear the “only in the Lord,” but we read “she is free to be married to whom she wishes,” and we no longer set beside it “only in the Lord.” And yet even there, when he said “only in the Lord,” he again checked the word saying she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment. So the apostle, having said the more auspicious thing—“For she is made holy”—left us to understand the other.

Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping God’s commandments. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). It will seem that he has unseasonably cast beside the word about marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about those from circumcision who believe not needing to draw the foreskin, and again those in uncircumcision not needing to be circumcised, and about “Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned,” and what follows. Perhaps then he took slavery and freedom as a paradigm of the married and the unmarried, calling circumcised the one who has put away the wife and uncircumcised the one who has married? For as the two will become one flesh and wife and husband are one flesh, and the circumcised has put away the things of the flesh, so the one who has put away the wife has as it were circumcised his own flesh; so also he calls a slave; for since he says also elsewhere the brother or the sister is not enslaved in such things, as if the married are slaves, through
